title.en: Language work for Wit and Wisdom: words, if-clauses, questions and a narrative essay

text.en: In the story, a clever bundle of sticks answered a proud scholar's challenge. Wit also lives in the way we use language: the right word for a sound, a sentence that imagines something that never happened, a question asked with the right tone. This lesson shows the language tools behind the unit.

keepEnglishTerms: past perfect + would have + past participle

text.en:
Writers use sound words to let you hear a scene. Words like murmur, mumble, thud, groan, rattle, gasped and whispered tell the reader how something sounds. Choose them to match the mood, for example a murmur of excitement spread through the class.
A compound word joins two or more words to make a new meaning. It can be closed, like sunlight or courtroom, hyphenated, like well-planned, or open, like paddy seeds. A dictionary tells you which form is correct.
Match words to make compounds such as quick-witted, soft-spoken, ill-tempered and common sense, and then use them in sentences to check that they fit.
An if-clause is the subordinate clause that states a condition; the main clause tells what happens. In 'If you like, I will try my best', the if-clause uses the simple present and the main clause uses will. The condition may or may not be fulfilled, and the sentence is about a possible future.
In 'If, by chance, something were to go wrong, our farmers would suffer', the if-clause uses the simple past and the main clause uses would. This imagines a situation that is hypothetical, not real. 'If I were invisible, I would sneak into the secret room' works the same way.
In 'If I had known this would happen, I would have chosen another day', the if-clause uses the past perfect and the main clause uses would have and a past participle. It describes what would have been done differently in a past situation that can no longer be changed.
Intonation is the rise and fall of your voice. 'Yes or no' questions end with a rising tone, as in 'Are you coming home?'. Question-word questions beginning with what, why, when, how, where or who end with a falling tone, as in 'When will you come home?'.
Keep the word order correct in questions: say 'Who is the cleverest character in the story?', not 'Who the cleverest character is in the story?'.
A narrative essay tells a personal or imagined experience. It has an introduction that sets the context, a body with events in order, with description and the narrator's feelings, and a turning point, and a conclusion that states the outcome and the lesson. It is written in the first person in simple, correct language.

problem.en: Complete each sentence correctly and say which kind of if-sentence it is: (a) If it rains tomorrow, we ___ (stay) indoors. (b) If I ___ (be) a bird, I would fly over the hills. (c) If you had listened carefully, you ___ (solve) the puzzle.

text.en: (a) If it rains tomorrow, we will stay indoors. The if-clause is in the simple present and the main clause has will.

why.en: This is a possible future, so use simple present + will.

text.en: (b) If I were a bird, I would fly over the hills. The if-clause uses the simple past form were and the main clause uses would.

why.en: This imagines something that is not true, so use simple past + would.

text.en: (c) If you had listened carefully, you would have solved the puzzle. The if-clause uses the past perfect and the main clause uses would have + past participle.

why.en: The situation is in the past and cannot be changed, so use past perfect + would have + past participle.

prompt.en: Explain the three kinds of if-sentences with one example each, and say how the voice should move in 'Where do you live?' and 'Do you live here?'.

requiredIdeas.en: Impossible past: past perfect + would have + past participle
Question-word questions fall; yes-no questions rise

commonMisconceptions.en: Using will in the if-clause itself
Using a rising tone for every question

points.en: Sound words, compound words (closed, hyphenated, open) enrich writing.
If-clauses: simple present + will (possible); simple past + would (imaginary); past perfect + would have + past participle (impossible past).
Yes-no questions have a rising tone; question-word questions a falling tone; keep question word order correct.
A narrative essay has an introduction, a body with a turning point and a conclusion with a lesson, in the first person.
